title: We released a 9B "news veto" model for trading bots that runs on an 8 GB Mac (MLX 8-bit + distilled 4-bit)
author: NovaeonStudio

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the eval I'd want isn't accuracy on the 495 held-out items, it's what the veto did to the bot. take every buy the bot wanted over the test window, split them into vetoed and not, and show the forward return of each pile. if the vetoed pile doesn't look worse, the classifier is right and it does not matter. also the labels came from a model reading a guide, so the held-out score measures agreement with that model, not with the market.

replies.author: NovaeonStudio
replies.body:
Ran it.

Setup: one year of backtest entries (Oct '25 – Sep '26, Binance perps, 20 coins, 1×, fees + funding), the bot's own news-check code, archived headlines instead of the live feeds. Date-only timestamps are shifted 24h so nothing leaks forward.

616 entries, 10 vetoed:

vetoed: −2.1% avg trade, 1/10 winners, −2.8% at 72h

allowed: +1.0% avg trade, 38% winners, +0.9% at 72h

The vetoed pile is worse. It's also only \~5 real events (Aave after the Kelp hack, the LTC MWEB exploit, the TAO founder dispute …), so I'm not calling it significant. Portfolio impact is flat (+61.4% vs +61.5%) because the stop already caps those trades at −2 to −5%. It's a tail guard, which is the job it has.

The more useful result came from checking coverage: the live bot only read four outlet feeds, and 17 of 20 coins had no headlines at all in a typical 48h window. So the veto was barely running. 1.1.1 is out and adds per-coin Google News searches, the same source the training data and this replay used, with slots reserved for risk-angle hits. Every coin now gets 12–15 headlines per check.

Code, report and per-trade CSVs: [github.com/tree/main/research/veto-eval](http://github.com/tree/main/research/veto-eval)

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: this is the right eval and the flat portfolio line is the honest result: the stop and the veto cover the same trades, so the veto only earns its keep when price gaps through the stop, which on exploit news is exactly when it does. the coverage finding is the bigger one. a veto that never sees a headline can't be measured at all.

replies.author: NovaeonStudio
replies.body:
Tested it. I re-priced every stop exit in the replay on the 1h candles, once filled halfway to the candle low and once at the low itself.

Only 5 of 616 entries hit the −10% stop in the year. Worst case at the low: −13.7% instead of −10.1%. More to the point: none of the 10 vetoed entries ever got near the stop. They would have left on the strategy's own exit at −1 to −5%. So in this data the veto isn't a stop-gap guard. It skips a handful of small losers, and the stop handles the rest.

The one case that fits your point is TAO on 2026-04-09. With the news timestamped when it broke, the veto blocks it; that trade was one of the five stop-outs. With the same news a day late, it goes through. So timeliness matters as much as coverage.

Caveat: a single year without a mid-trade exploit on one of the 20 coins. The tail you describe is real, it just didn't show up here.
